newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine press howls at Menem TV probe suspension.
newsitem.headline: Argentine press howls at Menem TV probe suspension.

text.p: An independent Argentine television channel's decision not to air an investigation into President Carlos Menem's grandiose building plans for his tiny home town sparked fierce debate on Thursday about censorship.

Journalists and opposition politicians said it was a clear case of censorship, but Menem's Peronist government denied reports they had leant on television channel America 2 not to air the programme "Two Voices" on Wednesday night.

Interior Minister Carlos Corach said it was the decision of the channel's owner Eduardo Eurnekian and it was "absurd" to speak of government pressure, since Menem himself ordered state channel ATC to offer to air the programme.

"Nobody in government had anything to do with this episode but since it's a matter of freedom of the press, the president ordered me to make this offer," Communications Secretary Raul Delgado told reporters.

America issued a statement saying it suspended the show because the investigation by the journalist Roman Lejtman, an outspoken critic of Menem's government, "had to be analysed in case its airing causes the channel legal problems."
Lejtman investigated Menem's projects in Anillaco, his home town in the northwestern desert province of La Rioja.
The Peronist chief has built a luxury home there, as well as a mountain refuge, an artificial lake for fishing, a zoo and a modern runway for a town of just 850 people.
Lejtman said he discovered the zoo was built on state property and Menem had flown in a U.S. explosives expert on his presidential jet "to blow up a mountain" to build it.

But Interior Minister Corach said it was "absurd" to make allegations about Menem's country home. "The president has been building his house for 12 years, long before he was president, so it makes no sense. And the runway is not for the president's house but for the town of Anillaco," Corach said.

The four journalists on "Two Voices", who hoped the report would be aired by another channel on Thursday, had no doubt it was scrapped because of "a very serious case of censorship," said presenter Marcelo Longobardi.

Press lobby group PERIODISTAS warned that the suspension of "Two Voices", together with the murder of news photographer Jose Luis Cabezas of Noticias magazine a month ago, "make for a worrying panorama for the future of Argentine democracy."
